articles.title: What If We Gave the Browser a Small Brain?
articles.excerpt: Here is a question that has been quietly haunting me: What is a browser actually capable of? We treat it as a window — a pane of glass we look through at software running somewhere else. Every "intell…
articles.body: Here is a question that has been quietly haunting me: What is a browser actually capable of? We treat it as a window — a pane of glass we look through at software running somewhere else. Every "intelligent" thing we do online follows the same ritual: our words, our photos, our files travel to a distant computer, something happens there, and the result travels back. The browser just displays it. But the device you are reading this on is a supercomputer by any historical standard, and the browser is the most widely deployed runtime in human history — sitting on billions of machines, capable of running real computation, and mostly used to render other people's servers. So the question sharpens into something more interesting: What if we gave the browser a small brain?
articles.author: JigsawLabs

articles.title: Maven Explained: Lifecycle, pom.xml and Dependencies
articles.excerpt: When I wrote my first real Java project, I had a folder of .java files, a folder of JAR files I had downloaded by hand and a very long javac command that I kept in a text file. When a teammate cloned…
articles.body: When I wrote my first real Java project, I had a folder of .java files, a folder of JAR files I had downloaded by hand and a very long javac command that I kept in a text file. When a teammate cloned the project, it didn't compile on their machine. Their JAR versions were different, their folders were different and the command had to be changed. That's the problem Maven solves. You describe your project in one file, and one short command builds it the same way on every machine: it downloads the libraries, compiles the code, runs the tests and packages everything into a JAR or WAR.

I came back to publish something about AI and coding teams, and the first thing I saw was this unpublished draft. I'm sharing it because of how extraordinarily relevant it still is. It's something we are actively combating. Yes, we need to be responsible. No, most of us aren't -- and it's mind-blowing that this is still out there. We're leaving it up to our tools to be safe, yet we're still the ones operating the controls. It's an incredibly beautiful dance we find ourselves in, and I wanted to share it. articles.body: Anthropic replaced Git with a custom centralized version control system called Scion after their commit rate jumped from 2,500 to 30,000 per day. The spike correlates directly with internal deployment of Fable and Mythos-class models. Claude is now the heaviest user of their source control infrastructure, and the system was explicitly designed around the assumption that agents are always online. This is not a story about better tooling. It is a story about how agent-generated code velocity breaks the assumptions baked into distributed version control. Why Git Could Not Scale Git's distributed model assumes developers work offline, clone full repositories, and merge infrequently.

articles.title: MovingLake's Bidirectional Connectors: How Real-Time ETL Agents Skip the Data Warehouse
articles.excerpt: Most reverse ETL tools assume you already have a data warehouse. You extract from production systems, load into Snowflake or BigQuery, transform in dbt, then push enriched records back to your CRM. Mo…
articles.body: Most reverse ETL tools assume you already have a data warehouse. You extract from production systems, load into Snowflake or BigQuery, transform in dbt, then push enriched records back to your CRM. MovingLake skips the warehouse entirely and pipes data straight from APIs to destination systems in both directions. For agentic workflows that need to read from third-party APIs and write decisions back to production databases without manual orchestration, this architecture exposes new failure modes and design trade-offs. What MovingLake Does MovingLake provides bidirectional data connectors that handle both traditional ETL (API to Snowflake) and reverse ETL (warehouse or API directly to CRM) in real time.

articles.title: SpaceX wants to launch Starship more than 450 times per year from South Texas
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has proposed increasing the number of allowed Starship launches from its Starbase site in South Texas from 25 per year to 456. The FAA is currently reviewing the request.
articles.body: SpaceX wants to start flying its Starship megarocket a lot more often. The company has requested permission to launch Starship from its Starbase site in South Texas up to 456 times per year. That's a big jump from the currently allowed cadence of 25. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the early stages of reviewing the request. Today (Oct. 14), the agency announced "its intent to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement, open a public scoping period and hold public scoping meetings for SpaceX’s proposal." Starship, which stands more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall, is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. It's also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX believes will revolutionize spaceflight.

articles.body: TL;DR The Motorola Signature 27 is scheduled to receive up to seven major Android OS updates and bi-monthly security updates for up to seven years. Some Motorola fans are fine with fewer, more stable updates, while others are more concerned about those two words: “up to.” Motorola’s software reputation has never quite matched the appeal of its hardware. Its phones can be fast, stylish, and packed with clever ideas, but software update support often becomes the part buyers grumble about later .

There’s Valkyra, Red Team; Manticore, Green Team; and Lonestar, Blue Team. They look different on the field, with Red rocking a soviet style, Green wearing Persian gear, and Blue looking like a Western paramilitary, but they all have access to the same equipment and have equal chance to win. articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions , had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China , impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up. Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
